results.query_title: Focus on Spark
results.query_body:
I have #16320/#16498 out to bring Spark up to existing standards for our examples. This bug is both a friction log of things I ran into while working on that PR, and a set of anticipated issues with Spark.

I organized this into two sections, Spark-specific-ish and Kubernetes-general. Some of these bullets have open issues and I'm documenting them as part of the vertical slice involved.

**Please** feel free to correct me if I messed something up obvious about Spark or Kubernetes. I was a former Spark user in a bygone era, but it's moved quite quickly since then so any expertise has rusted.
## Spark specific
- [x] **Where?**: #17027 talks about whether this even belongs in [INLINE_CODE], since it works over multiple versions, and isn't a _teaching_ example.
- [ ] **Config**: #16320 puts up a static configuration of Spark. [The Spark configuration alone](http://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/configuration.html) is pretty large, and that's not including [the Hadoop configuration](https://hadoop.apache.org/docs/current/hadoop-project-dist/hadoop-common/ClusterSetup.html) that also influences it. It's difficult to say what a customer would actually want to tune in production, but it's clear that treating Spark as a fully black-box is probably wrong (but has legs for a while). Don't get me wrong, it's not unreasonable to offer an out-of-the-box configuration that just works, but we're going to need a way to inload configuration. In this case, the container is also going to need to compose configuration with the configuration that "just works" (i.e. as a simple example, if we took in a secret for additional [INLINE_CODE], we should probably just splat the existing configuration together, or compose them to allow the additional config to override KVs in the base image). See #6477, #4822.
- [ ] **Jar Files**: We're going to need a way to quickly compose base images and other modules. See #831.
- [ ] **Parameterized Resources**: It's not clear how to merge [spark](../tree/master/examples/spark) and [spark-gluster](../tree/master/examples/spark/spark-gluster). The long term answer is probably things like #10527, #11492, etc. Short term, one option might be to assume that you have _some_ storage available that can be mounted as [INLINE_CODE] and instead of assuming gluster, we rewrite the example as either gluster or NFS and use a PV claim. But that's not the only example of a resource that needs to be parameterized / templatized in some fashion.
- [ ] **Pod Local Storage**: The existing example doesn't override [INLINE_CODE], so it's only useful for certain workloads, namely in-memory only workloads. This used to be the bread-and-butter of Spark because it was all it could do, but it proved rather limiting not to spill. However, using network or distributed storage for Spark intermediate storage is somewhat naive, but is the most convenient way on our system to configure a ReplicationController for storage. But, for the short term, given that the replication controller itself is [INLINE_CODE] wide, for anyone in GCE we could add a script to this directory to provision a set of [INLINE_CODE] volumes and use a claim to resolve it.
- [ ] **Storage Testing**: Spark doesn't necessarily need storage that will outlive the life of the pod (if you blow away a worker on a running job it will recompute the RDD around it, as you'd expect, since storage within Spark is largely annotated caching with [INLINE_CODE] and shuffle-spill, both of which are losable). The pod case is different than e.g. [Netflix's Chaos Monkey with Spark](http://techblog.netflix.com/2015/03/can-spark-streaming-survive-chaos-monkey.html) tests, though, because the pod comes back with a different name.
- [ ] **Scheduling**: I kept Spark configured in Standalone mode with a fixed width ReplicationController for the worker pool. There's a lot of really long, interesting conversations to have how to handle this correctly. Mesos does a lot here with fine-grained scheduling to pick up slack capacity on the cluster, YARN integrates slightly differently, we could still take yet another. (Obviously a large TBD bullet.)
- [ ] **Resiliency**: I put some basic liveness probes on the master/workers, but there's some obvious stuff missing: (a) The master either needs to be running in [INLINE_CODE] mode (easiest) or (b) in multi-master backed by ZooKeeper (hardest) in order to withstand a restart with a running application. Similarly, the driver pod itself isn't protect at all right now, but before we protect that, we just want to look at the driver mode, how we want to support Spark app submission in the cluster, and the Zeppelin bullet below.
- [ ] **Test**: If we actually want to productionize an app, we really should have tests of some sort.
- [x] **Zeppelin**: We should definitely get [Zeppelin](https://zeppelin.incubator.apache.org/) working. I morphed the current example into an example familiar to Googlers, a Shakespeare word count example, but it's using the pyspark driver and lacks "pop".
- [ ] **Spark UI**: The Spark WebUI worker links won't work because they're cluster IPs. Spark presents it's worker IPs as if they're globally accessible, not anticipating that we're proxying the connection to the master's WebUI (which seems like an utterly sane). We could obviously proxy all of the worker webuis as well, but Spark doesn't seem to support a URL-rewrite scheme for the master WebUI page, so we'd probably have to slap an nginx proxy in front of it. (See #16949 for one way to maybe solve it.)
## Kubernetes general
- [ ] **Pod Hostname/Service Mismatch**: During the conversion from a [INLINE_CODE] pod to a [INLINE_CODE] single-pod-replication-controller, the Spark master objected to the slaves because the master started with a hostname that didn't match the service name the slaves were contacting it on. In this case, the slaves connected to the DNS [INLINE_CODE], and [INLINE_CODE] saw messages for [INLINE_CODE] and said "nope, that ain't me, I'm [INLINE_CODE], you must have me confused for someone else". (c.f. #386)
- [ ] **Environment Variable Injection Issues**: If you're not actually using the service environment variables, injection can actually throw you off when an environment variable from Docker or Kubernetes overrides something that a vendor script was expecting. For example, I had a service named [INLINE_CODE], which resulted in [INLINE_CODE], which is an environment variable that the Spark [INLINE_CODE] script will happily pick up. Unfortunately, the script was expecting a single integer, not [INLINE_CODE]. It would be nice if there was a way to disable service env variable injection. See #1768 (which seems to cover that possibility, maybe).
- [ ] **Best Practices Friction**: [Config best practices](../tree/fe6b15ba/docs/user-guide/config-best-practices.md) is at odds with [how we test examples currently](../tree/fe6b15ba/examples/examples_test.go): The resources probably belong in the same file, but I didn't do it that way because of the example schema test. See #16444, just filed.
- [ ] **Slow Dev Iteration**: This was probably the longest I've spent iterating on an ensemble of Docker containers, and I found it somewhat painful (until I automated it slightly) to bump the tag in the Makefile, bumping it in the [INLINE_CODE], etc. Our best practices seem to suggest using image hardcoded tags (which make sense), and I probably would've scripted it further if I had to go much longer. The process itself before presenting a PR is interesting because prior to a PR you basically end up "hiding" the entire thing on a private project, then you end up displaying one "bump" to the world. Do we have any issues discussing how to iterate on "the package" (the set of [INLINE_CODE], Dockerfiles, etc.)? As we get anyhere near packaging, that's going to be one killer feature - the ability to rapidly iterate on actually developing package blobs for k8s (the resources and images both).

cc @davidopp @timstclair @timothysc @wattsteve

results.query_title: RFC: Determine the scalability goal for v1.2 kubelet
results.query_body:
The umbrella issue for kubelet's scalability: #12540

Kubelet manages and monitors all user pods on a node to ensure their container states meet the desired pod specifications. Every pod and/or container Kubelet manages incurs a certain resource overhead even in the absence of active events (i.e., no spec change or container lifecycle events). The exact per-pod overhead varies based on the detailed pod specification, but in general, such steady-state management overhead of is proportional to the number of active pods/containers. When there no active pods, the resource overhead should be negligible.

Below are some resource usage numbers for the v1.1 kubelet.
## v1.1 Resource Usage*\* (commit: dd1187c3ff9a5)

Cluster setup/workload:
- Three n1-standard-2 nodes on GCE (i.e., 2-core)
- Running all default cluster add-on pods
- 0 and 40 single-container pause pods per node
- 30-minutes measurement period
- The cpu usage numbers are aggregated by ~~10s~~ **_1s**_ intervals
- The working set memory size was hard to measured correctly (see #12422 for details). In the experiments, I set logging level to 0 and lowered the cgroup memory limit of kubelet and docker to create a constant memory pressure, then let them bounce back until the usage was stable. The numbers are approximates and should only be considered as ballparks.
### 0 pause pods per node

| | median cpu | 95th% cpu | memory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| kubelet | 0.02 | 0.05 | 35MB |
| docker | 0.01 | 0.03 | 35MB |
| kube-proxy | <0.001 | 0.01 | <5MB* |
### 40 pause pods per node

| | median cpu | 95th% cpu | memory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| kubelet | 0.18 | 0.64 | 55MB |
| docker | 0.01 | 0.62 | 70MB |
| kube-proxy | <0.001 | 0.03 | <5MB* |

_kube-proxy’s memory usage depends on the number of services in the cluster. In this test case, the number of services is 7._

Note that, kubelet syncs all pods periodically, hence even though the median cpu usage tends to be lower, the cpu spikes are significant.
### 90 pause pods per node?

v1.1 does not support 90 pods per node, but I did some rough measurement and the median cpu usage of kubelet and docker combined varies from 0.35 to 1.2 cores -- it was right on the edge of a steep curve. Beyond 70th%, it was consistently > 1.4 core.
### Reaction latency

The latency Kubelet takes to notice a container event (e.g. died) varies and could be up to **10+** seconds, since the sync period is 10s.
## v1.2 Resource Usage Target

For v1.2 we want to set a goal so that we can work towards to it. The goal would affect what approach we pick to tackle the issues.

Below are some tentative targets. Suggestions/comments are welcome.
- Number of pods: 90 pause pods + all add-on pods
- Reaction latency (for majority of the container evens): within 3s
 - This is somewhat arbitrary. We have a pretty long reaction latency today, and we can certainly lower this more _if_ we adopt the docker event stream (#16831). What's an acceptable value?
- cpu usage for kubelet and docker combined:
 - median: 0.2 core (10% of the 2-core machine)
 - 95th%: 0.6 core
 - 99th%: TBD
## Caveats
- The detailed pod spec may affect the resource usage. For example, if every container defines a health check, the overhead of periodic probing may significantly increase the cpu usage. We should also publish the usage numbers of the worst-case scenario.
- We focus on the steady-state resource usage. When there are non-monitoring work involved (e.g. container creation/deletion), the cpu usage would of course increase. We can further restrict the usage by either rate-limiting operations, or set a reasonable cpu share for kubelet and docker. Again, this is not the focus of the issue.
- The built-in cadvisor constantly monitors all containers stats. The cpu usage of cadvisor for 100 pods is not ideal (see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/16296#issuecomment-152365160), but seems tolerable at the moment. We will optimize that if it becomes the bottleneck.
- We will want to optimize the 99th% cpu usage later as well. The current measurements are not very meaningful because kubelet and docker each consumes ~1 core at 99th% cpu usage.
- If we use a smaller cpu measurement interval, we might be able to capture the fine-grained, more dynamic behavior. On the other hand, the measurement overhead would increase.
- The goal will be specifically for docker, but the most of the improvement will apply to rkt as well.

/cc @kubernetes/goog-node

results.query_title: RFC: Where to put official Kubernetes packages / templates / etc.?
results.query_body:
We're starting work on building more baked, fully formed sets of resources and images running on Kubernetes (see #16517, which is still very much in pre-alpha, but defines an epoch to get Spark to a respectable place). Right now, we (the Kubernetes team) have been checking the pieces for this into the [INLINE_CODE] directory into the main https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes repo. That's starting to feel wrong for a few reasons:
- The collection of resources and images for "apps" might use advanced features that only exist on [INLINE_CODE], but typically are designed to work back to old versions. If they _do_ use advanced features, typically I would suggest templatizing it somehow (more on that in a bit).
- There's a fundamental difference between teaching examples, and packages. For instance, you might use [INLINE_CODE] to teach Services, but an [INLINE_CODE] package may actually look pretty different (it should include a [INLINE_CODE], once it exists, and more metadata in general). Teaching examples don't have to be full-blown apps, and full-blown apps don't have to teach.

In addition, we've now got both [Deployment Manager](https://github.com/kubernetes/deployment-manager), [Helm](https://github.com/deis/helm) and [OpenShift Templates](https://docs.openshift.org/latest/dev_guide/templates.html) as interesting targets to write templates/packages for. It'd be nice to package this metadata in one place with the package. ~~(Unfortunately, helm (unlike DM) can't point at an alternate git path, so that one is actually tricky/possibly wasteful to consolidate under our repo as well. This is possibly a temporary limitation, though.)~~

**Current Proposal**:
- Create a https://github.com/kubernetes/application-dm-templates repo to host Deployment Manager templates, satisying https://github.com/kubernetes/deployment-manager/issues/82, splitting it from https://github.com/kubernetes/deployment-manager for all the reasons laid out in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/17027#issuecomment-157785896.
- Create a https://github.com/kubernetes/application-images repo to host image build content for containerized applications: Dockerfiles, startup scripts, config files, etc.

Both of these can be maintained by (separate) teams with fairly open memberships.

If there is interest in an additional repository to host Helm charts, we can create such a repo, but for the upstream https://github.com/helm/charts is the obvious spot. Similarly, if there is interest in hosting OpenShift templates, we can create such a repo, but the upstream https://github.com/openshift/origin/tree/master/examples is the obvious spot. We will link there in the k8s docs as well.

cc @brendandburns @bgrant0607 @aronchick @kubernetes/sig-big-data @jackgr

results.query_title: Proposal: Authorizing use of a PodSecurityPolicy via the "Use" verb
results.query_body:
## Summary of proposal
- a pod has a pointer to a serviceAccount. (this is currently the case)
- a user must be authorized to **use** a serviceAccount in order to create a pod that has that serviceAccountName. (proposed new check)
- a user must be authorized to **use** a podSecurityPolicy in order to create a serviceAccount that points to that podSecurityPolicy. (proposed new check)
- a serviceAccount has a pointer to a PodSecurityPolicy (proposed new field)
- a pod's PodSecurityContext and each of its container's SecurityContext must match the Pod's serviceAccount's PodSecurityPolicy. (proposed new check)
## Longer Version
- (prerequisite) @deads2k's proposal #12209 is implemented, in particular so that:
 - the Authorization interface knows the specific verb (e.g."create" or "logs") used.
 - the Authorization interface knows the name and namespace of the referenced object.
- (prerequisite) @pweil-'s proposal #7893 for PodSecurityPolicy is merged, except the [INLINE_CODE] and [INLINE_CODE] fields are dropped from it.
- (new thing) "serviceAccount" gets a new verb called "use". The endpoint does not do anything, it is just for authorization purposes.
- (new thing) when a pod is created or updated by user U, and the pod has a serviceAccount S, then, in addition to our existing authorization checks, there is a new, second, authorization check that checks whether user U is allowed to "use" serviceAccount S.
 this check happens after an empty ServiceAccount is defaulted to "default".
- (new thing) serviceAccounts gain an objectReference to a PodSecurityPolicy. 
 (new thing) an admission controller enforces that a pod's securityContext(s) and podSecurityContext must match the podSecurityPolicy of its serviceAccount.
## Detailed design
### Pod Creation Detailed Steps
1. request authenticated
2. modify authenticated user using "acting-as", if requested, for e.g. controller managers (see #16933, not strictly needed for this proposal but included to show all steps in eventual system)
3. check whether authenticated user U (in groups G) is allowed to create pods, in the general case, via [INLINE_CODE]
4. LimitRanger admission controller runs (per #17097, this may someday set security-sensitive fields, hence we ought to re-authorize after defaulting)
5. SecurityContextDeny plugin no longer used
6. ServiceAccount plugin may set default serviceAccount
7. Note: this marks the end of "mutating" admission controllers. All further admission controllers are not allowed to modify the object from the request body. Since the object is in its final form, the next step(s) can do final authorization of the object.
8. New UseServiceAccount admission controller checks whether authenticated user U (in groups G) is allowed to use the pod's service account S, via [INLINE_CODE] 
9. New PodSecurityPolicyCheck plugin compares the pod's securityContext(s) and podSecurityContext with the pod's serviceAccount's podSecurityPolicy, and rejects if not matching
10. DenyEscalatingExec is not needed anymore, since it is covered by UseServiceAccount check.
11. Quota admission controller runs.
### The "UseServiceAccount" admission controller
- for "create", "update", "exec", and "attach" verbs, it checks that the requesting user is authorized to "use" the serviceAccount of the Pod in question.
- for "logs", it does not make this check. reasoning here is that sensitivity of logs (PII or not) is somewhat independent of the privileges of the pod that is doing the logging. So, don't require the check. 
- for "portforward", "proxy" verbs: TBD
- for "status" verb, no check.
### Use cases from #7893
##### Use case 1

As an administrator, I can create a namespace for a person that can't create privileged containers AND enforces that the UID of the containers is set to a certain value

steps to implement use case:
- create namespace N1
- create PodSecurityPolicy P1 specifying desired UID.
- create service account S1 in N1, pointing to P1.
- allow user U1 to "do anything to pods in N1" and to "use S1".
##### Use case 2:

As a cluster operator, an infrastructure component should be able to create a pod with elevated
privileges in a namespace N where regular users cannot create pods with these privileges or execute
commands in that pod.

steps to implement use case:
- create totally permissive PodSecurityPolicy P2 which can create privileged pods.
- create special purpose service account S2 which references P2
- give cluster operator user U2 permission to use S2
- do not give any other users permission to use S2. Create S2 in a namespace other than N2 if needed.
- U2 creates Pod with service account S2, and any security context desired.

Note that the cluster admin can (1) make a powerful service account and make a pod using that account or (2) make a pod that runs as any existing service account, with that service accounts limitations, but the cluster admin cannot make a powerful pod that runs as an existing weak service account. This is the same as Unix. Root is powerful when running as root, and can su to any other user, but it not powerful when su'ed to a weak user.
#### Reasons I like this approach
- We will need to add code that checks whether a user can read a secret before allowing creation of a pod that mounts it. The pattern for that will be quite similar to this. If we do #7893 as proposed, then we end up with two quite different patterns.
- It will be easier to teach an existing outside-of-kubernetes authorization system that something called a "serviceAccount" has a "use" verb, than it will be to teach it about the exact format of a PSP object and its users and groups fields.
- Keeps users and groups (which belong to "object-level authorization") separate from field-level authorization (see #17549). 
- The "use" verb idea is very similar to the "acting-as" header proposed in #16933 to avoid confused deputy problem.
- By putting a reference to PodSecurityPolicy into a serviceAccount, it allows you to know the maximum set of things that a serviceAccount can do from inspecting just that serviceAccount object. Otherwise, you can have a privileged pod run by a serviceAccount that you don't expect to be privileged.
- Once the pod's service account has been determined, further policy checks need not make any reference to users or groups. This should simplify pod policy.
- Rather than needing to check all the PSPs a user has access to, the correct PSP is known from the pod's SA.

figure out how this would work with network policy.

results.query_body:
### Idea

Make it easy to export "local" files as a (limited lifetime) volume which pods in a kubernetes cluster can mount. 
### Use cases
##### Interactive Development

I am developing an interpreted program such as a python or node.js program. I want to use the editor/IDE on my desktop. But I want to run the program in a pod because it relies on things that exist in the kubernetes environment, and not my desktop (e.g. DNS, service account credentials, services, more memory/cpu, etc). I want to avoid the step of rebuilding an image and restarting a pod every time I make an edit. I want a solution like this:
1. I develop my source files locally in my [INLINE_CODE] directory. 
2. I export [INLINE_CODE] as remote storage that can be mounted by Pods. It contains my source code (e.g. [INLINE_CODE]).
3. I [INLINE_CODE] a pod that has an image that includes my interpreter, like [INLINE_CODE], but not my source code. The pod also mounts the exported volume ( [INLINE_CODE]), which contains the source code. The command line is set in the pod spec to [INLINE_CODE] so I can run via [INLINE_CODE].
4. I use [INLINE_CODE] to connect to the pod and then run [INLINE_CODE]. 
5. In another window, I make edits on my local host, using my editor.
6. Then I restart the program in the [INLINE_CODE] session.
##### Porcelain for Docker-like experience

People use to docker may ask why [INLINE_CODE] has no equivalent to [INLINE_CODE]. 

We could add a [INLINE_CODE] option to [INLINE_CODE] which would automate the process of exporting <local-path> and add the needed volume mounts to the Pod spec.
### Proposed New Commands

When a user runs [INLINE_CODE], the following things happen:
1. [INLINE_CODE] generates a credential that will be used by clients to access the local fileserver.
2. [INLINE_CODE] posts the secret to the current namespace with a generated name.
3. [INLINE_CODE] starts a file server (e.g. forks a process or starts a goroutine, implementation TBD) that serves the files under <path> on a port of the local machine's public IP. This fileserver is exposed to the internet, in typical use cases. The fileserver is protected by the credential from the first step.
4. when the user hits ctrl-c, [INLINE_CODE] stops the file server and cleans up the secret.

When a user runs [INLINE_CODE], then the following things happen:
1. pod spec is generated, as it currently is for [INLINE_CODE]
2. steps 1, 2 and 3 from [INLINE_CODE] happen
3. pod spec is patched to add an item to [INLINE_CODE] with the appropriate volume type. 
 1. appropriate volume type depends on the implementation we choose
 2. the volumeSpec references to the appropriate secret (the one from previous step), e.g. how [INLINE_CODE] has a [INLINE_CODE].
 3. the volumeSpec specifies its server (e.g. [INLINE_CODE]) as the local hostname and the port chosen in the previous step)
4. pod spec is patched to add an item to the [INLINE_CODE], using the added volumeSpec and the user-specified [INLINE_CODE].
5. cleanup as in [INLINE_CODE] when run is done.
### Implementation alternatives

NFS mounting is probably most widely supported volume type (see #16741). 

NFS server distribution options:
- rely on kernel nfs server
 - won't work on windows, and maybe not on Mac.
- nfs server as a library written in pure go, run as a goroutine in kubectl
 - could not find an existing pure go NFS server.
- nfs server as a library in c, linked via cgo, run as a goroutine in kubectl.
 - changes our build process to build gco, could be headache for cross-platform builds
- ship an extra binary with kubectl that it will fork, which runs a userspace nfs daemon 
 - pain to ship extra binary with kubectl
- kubectl launches a userspace NFS server in a docker container
 - requires docker on the users machine, but most users will have docker for building images.
 - can use a containerized userspace nfs server such as https://github.com/macadmins/unfs3 
 - seems like best option

Alternative to NFS would be FUSE volume type on the client. The fuse module could talk whatever protocol (e.g. https) to the server, which can be written in pure go and linked into kubectl. 

Nodes inside the cluster may be firewalled making it difficult for them to reach the kubectl-user's local machine via NFS protocol. Some kind of proxy or tunnel may be needed too.

results.query_title: Support zookeeper in PetSet
results.query_body:
**I haven't deployed zookeeper to production, I'll incorporate comments from anyone who has into this missive.**

Zookeeper exposes a filesystem like api similar to chubby or etcd. Write requests sent to followers are forwarded to the leader, which executes then broadcasts the result as a proposed state change to all servers in the ensemble. Servers respond with an ACK, leader only waits for a quorum of ACKs before committing.
### Initial Deployment

Initial deployment of zookeeper is quite easy because the members of the ensemble will poll on a timeout for peers to show up. Each server takes its configuration from a zoo.cfg file that contains a total list of servers (including itself), and a myid file that contains its own identity in zoo.cfg.

Kube implementation notes:
1. Create a service with ClusterIP: None and name zk.
2. Create 3 RCs, with the pod.beta.kubernetes.io/hostname and subdomain set to, eg: "server$(ID)", "zk"
3. Each RC/replica has a unique ID. The id is used in 2 places:
 - zoo.cfg: this is a list of all peers, including this replica
 - myid: this reflects the index in zoo.cfg of the current replica
4. Each RC/replica has a pvc that stores its data files and transaction log.
### Scaling
#### Standalone to quorum

A standalone member needs to restart in quorum mode with the right configuration.
#### Observers

Zookeeper has a role called "Observer" that allows the scaling of reads by adding members that don't participate in voting. Adding observers is easier than adding followers. Observers still proxy writes to master.
1. Write all server config files with server.$(observer id):ip:observer.
2. Write observer config file with peerType=observer.
#### Core members

Scaling core members is somewhat brittle. The first option that springs to mind is: shutdown the 3 member cluster, bring up a 5 member cluster. This is racy because of the following scenario:
- A,B,C steady state cluster
- C lags, A,B are in quorum
- Shutdown cluster
- A,B,C,D,E cluster started
- A,B are slow to start
- C,D,E form quorum and accept some writes
- A,B come up, erase state that C didn't initially have

Newer releases of zookeeper have a "reconfig" command to help with this dance.
1. Make sure there is quorum.
2. Join new members as non-participants, so they sync state with master but don't vote.
3. Run zkCli.sh reconfig -add

The third step will promote non-participants specified after "add" to participants, commit the new config, and link it from the existing config through the "dynamicConfigFile" variable.

In older release, this needs to be done manually. Points to note when doing so:
- It's only safe to scale one member at a time. 
- If the joiner reboots during 3, the babysitter will have to clear out the config file, leaving it in a corrupt state confuses the ensemble. 
- One needs to be careful that the new joiner/joiners don't somehow form a quorum with a lagging follower. This involves listing them as observers and promoting them to participants (TODO elaborate on how this is done manually). 
- There are other situations where admin intervention maybe necessary to recover the cluster consistently, see: https://zookeeper.apache.org/doc/trunk/zookeeperReconfig.html#sc_reconfig_modifying for details. 
#### Hierarchical quorum

AKA deploying another zookeeper cluster and reconfiguring existing clusters to perform a weighted quorum. The weights of each group need to be computed by the admin or babysitter to distribute voting rights. All writes go to the leader, then out to the periphery, and a reply is stalled till a quorum replies from each group (this actually depends on the configured weights).

TODO: Update how one goes from normal to co-loc/hierarchical quorum and if that incurs downtime. Docs don't help clarify: https://zookeeper.apache.org/doc/r3.3.4/zookeeperInternals.html#sc_quorum. Can this be done by a generic autoscaler? 
### Upgrade

Very similar to etcd upgrade. See #23790. Babysitter needs to be careful in upgrading, you can't just eg: jump to version 3.5.0 without first updating to 3.4.6 (https://zookeeper.apache.org/doc/trunk/zookeeperReconfig.html#ch_reconfig_upgrade).
### Failures

Observer crash: all observers can crash and this will only affect read throughput.
Follower crash: as long as there's a quorum, the ensemble doesn't care about follower crash.
Leader crash: incurs downtime because new leaders will not start till there is agreement on the inital state of the epoch.
### Thoughts

Easier:
- Bootstrap as a static cluster. 
- Scale read throughput by adding observers.
- Update, as long as there isn't a version chain dependency. 
- Take down and rehabilitate a single server.

Harder: 
- Scale for write throughput by adding core members
- Re shuffle clients evenly across new members
- Distribute failures across a WAN (hierarchical groups)
- Take proactive action on failure

Some way to send an interrupt to existing replicas with some json about a new member might help with the harder points.

results.query_title: Detailed Design for Volume Mount/Unmount Redesign
results.query_body:
# Objective
- Rapid pod creation, deletion, and recreation for pods that require volume attaching/detaching/mounting/unmounting should never fail because of attach/detach/mount/unmount issues.
- Volumes that are attached/mounted should be gracefully handled on kubelet restart.
 - Issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/19953
- Two or more pods scheduled to the same node with the same volume should never fail (as long as it is allowed by the volume plugin’s AccessModes policy).
 - Issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/19953
- When a volume is attached to the node in read-only mode, and the pod referencing it is deleted and another pod referencing the volume is quickly created in read-write mode, then the volume should detached and reattached in the correct (read-write) mode.
 - Issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/11879
- One or more pods referencing different partitions of the same volume should not fail (as long as it doesn’t violate volume plugin’s AccessModes policy).
 - Issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/20835
# Background

In the existing Kubernetes design the kubelet is responsible for determining what volumes to attach/mount and detach/unmount from the node it is running on.

The loop in Kubelet that is responsible for attaching and mounting volumes (the pod creation loop) is separate from and completely independent (on a separate thread) of the loop that is responsible for unmounting and detaching volumes (orphaned volumes loop). This leads to race conditions between the asynchronous pod creation and orphaned volumes loops.

Although there is some logic in the GCE PD, AWS, and Cinder plugins to make sure that the actual attach/detach operations don’t interrupt each other, there is no guarantee as to the order of the operations themselves. So, for example, when a pod is created and then rapidly deleted and recreated, kubelet attaches and mounts the pod, then (if the second attach operation is triggered before the detach operation, which often happens) kubelet will execute the second attach operation successfully (since the disk is already attached), and the pending detach operation will then result in a disk-in-use being unmounted (which appears like data loss to user).

To mask this behavior, kubelet currently fails attach operations if the disk is already attached. This allows the second attach operation to fail, and the subsequent detach operation to succeed; further retries of the attach operation then succeed.

Although this workaround masks a nasty bug (apparent data loss to the end user), it results in other unwanted behavior (bugs):
1. When a kubelet is restarted, pods with volumes that are already attached will fail to start, because attempts by kubelet to attach a volume that is already attached continuously fail (since the volume is already attached).
2. When two or more pods specify the same volume (allowed for some plugins in certain cases), the second pod will fail to start because because the volume attach call for the 2nd pod will continuously fail since the volume is already attached (by the first pod).

The Volume/Attach Detach Controller design (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/20262) plans to move the attach/detach logic from kubelet to master, however the kubelet will still be responsible for mounting/unmounting (and, for backwards compatibility reasons, attach/detach in some cases), therefore these issues must be addressed.
# Solution Overview

Introduce a new asynchronous loop, called the volume manager loop, in kubelet that handles attach/detach and mount/unmount in a serialized manner. The existing orphaned volumes loop will be removed, and the logic for unmounting/detaching volumes will be moved to the volume manager loop. Similarly, the logic for determining which volumes to mount/attach will be moved from the pod creation loop to the volume manager loop. The pod creation loop will simply poll the new volume manager until its volumes are ready for use (attached and mounted).
# Detailed Design

The volume manager will maintain an in-memory cache containing a list of volumes that are required by the node (i.e. volumes that are referenced by pods scheduled to the node that the kubelet is running on). Each of these volumes will, in addition to the volume name, specify if the volume is mounted in read-only mode, and list the pods referencing the volume. This cache defines the state of the world according to the volume manager. This cache must be thread-safe.

On initial startup, the volume manager will read the [INLINE_CODE] and [INLINE_CODE] directories to figure out which volumes were attached and mounted to the node before it went down and pre-populate the in-memory cache.
### Primary Control Loop

The volume manager will have a loop that does the following:
- Fetch a copy of all pod and mirror pod objects from kubelet via pod manager.
- Acquire a lock on the in-memory cache.
- Search for new pods by iterating through the fetched pods, and for each pod with a [INLINE_CODE] [INLINE_CODE] check the volumes it defines or references (dereferencing any [INLINE_CODE] to fetch associated [INLINE_CODE] objects). For each of these volume:
 - If the volume _is not_ already in-memory cache (indicating a new volume has been discovered), then:
 - **Trigger “attach volume and mount device” logic** (detailed in section below) to attach the volume to the node and mount it to the main mount location.
 - A matching volume must also match access mode. For example, if a volume was attached in read-only mode, a new pod referencing the same volume in read-write mode, will be treated as a separate volume (this enables the scenario mentioned in objectives above).
 - If the volume is _already tracked_ in memory cache (indicating it is already attached and mounted to main location), then:

- Loop through all cached volumes and **trigger “unmount device and detach volume” logic** (detailed below) for any volumes that are no longer needed (exist in-memory cache but have no pods listed under them, indicating no running pods using the volume).

Attach, detach, mount, and unmount operations can take a long time to complete, so the primary volume manager loop should not block on these operations. Instead the primary loop should spawn new threads for these operations. The number of threads that can be spawned will be capped (possibly using a thread pool) and once the cap is hit, subsequent requests will have to wait for a thread to become available.

To prevent multiple attach/detach or mount/unmount operations on the same volume, the main thread will maintain a table mapping volumes to currently active operations.

results.query_title: Kubernetes logging, journalD, fluentD, and Splunk, oh my!
results.query_body:
In order to run k8s in our environment, I need to get logging information into Splunk. I need to pick up node logs AND application logs. I know at this point there is no drop-in solution, so I know i'll need to hack something together. 

What I'm seeking in this issue is not a 'here's the solution', though that would be great of course. 

I'm seeking advice on which of several solutions I've come up with are most likely to work, given how Kubernetes is evolving. 
## Research and references

Issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/1071 seems to have resulted in the current ability to choose 'elasticsearch' as a provider in kube-up.sh

Issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/17183 seems to indicate that the future is not yet clear.

Issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/23782 contemplates some limitations of the current approach also

Issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/21285 provides a proxy to send data to AWS instead of ES

Based on many sources, it seems clear that systemd/journalctl is the future of logging in *nix. latest versions of RHEL/Centos/Fedora and Ubuntu have moved this way.

While i'm of course willing to hack, i'd really rather avoid needing to re-build the k8s images if possible.
## Option 1 -- k8s->fluentd-->splunk

I could use fluentd, and then use a fluentd splunk plugin. If I use kube-up.sh with KUBERNETES_LOGGING_DESTINATION='elasticsearch', I get a fluentd/ES setup. There are plugins for fluentd that can forward content on to splunk.

But i do not know how i would configure k8s to NOT install elasticsearch as a part of startup. I also think this represents an extra layer of forwarding i'd rather avoid. With this solution, I think i would need to send all application output to STDOUT/STDERR, since this is how k8s currently gathers stuff. This solution does not use journald, which causes me to think this option is a doomed-to-change-in-the-near-future. Which leads me to option 2
## Option 2-- k8s->journald, docker->journald

I could forward all logs ( from the nodes and pods too ) to journalD using the docker journald log driver, and then capture data out of the journald logs and send to splunk from there. Honestly this seems like the 'right' solution. Why re-invent logging capture? If not already true, any strong security setup is going to require use of centralized logging capture, and that will need to be based on journald. 

There are two problems with this, though: 
1. doing it this way will not allow kubernetes metadata to be included in the log stream, and 
2. I believe this will break kubectl logs, because it relies on the docker json logs.
## Option 3 -- docker -> k8s -> journald

Logging directly from docker to journald means there isnt a chance to add k8s meta. What might be the coolest option is if k8s provided a docker logging driver that then proxies the data and sends it to journald. That way, as a system administrator, i just need to go to one place to get all my logs-- the journald service on each node. But i still get the k8s metadata too.

I have no reasonable ability to execute this option though, it would be a big change. But i'd be willing to help if this is a good way to do it.
## Option 4-- splunk docker log driver

http://blogs.splunk.com/2015/12/16/splunk-logging-driver-for-docker/

results.query_title: Make API field defaulting and validation less error-prone
results.query_body:
There are frequent errors in API field specification, such as:
- default vs inferred (e.g., [INLINE_CODE]: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/api/v1/types.go#L557); note that implicitly inferred is discouraged
- default vs required
- required/optional vs omitempty
- omitempty vs. pointers
- documentation vs actual defaulting and validation code

For examples of multiple errors in one type, see:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/18885#issuecomment-218376807

One way to make defaulting and validation less error prone would to be allow them to be specified declaratively, on API fields using tags or comments. Protocol buffers allow literal default values to be specified (though, unlike in Kubernetes, they aren't conveyed on the wire; non-literals, such as fields defaulted from other fields, can't be specified this way). Declarative validation, where possible (i.e., simple rules), was previously requested by #8116. 

Since omitempty and pointer rules are apparently non-obvious, I think we should require specification of required vs optional and then either verify that the other properties are consistent or autogenerate them. 

Auto-fixing field names in documentation is covered by #19319.

results.query_title: rkt networking discussion
results.query_body:
There are a number of small pieces of discussion scattered across this and the rkt repository related to how to handle networking setup; I'd like to consolidate this discussion here, talk about all the issues and options I know about, and hopefully figure out what the best option is.

Discussion refs:
https://github.com/coreos/rkt/issues/2249
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/26081
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/25404#issuecomment-218402169
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/24688
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/21923
And quite possibly several more I missed
## Introduction

Kubernetes and rkt both make use of CNI to configure container network namespaces. Each has independent means of configuring and executing plugins. Kubernetes also has a number of features that relate somewhat to the network namespace, such as availability of the pod's IP in a number of locations (status, downwards API, etc).

Until recently, rkt's handled network configuration on its own with no regard for Kubernetes' network logic. As of #25062, it was changed such that kubelet handles network setup and configuration for rkt. Unfortunately, both of these solutions have problems.

Below, the problems with each approach are listed. Finally, some paths forwards are suggested.
## Issues
- The PodIP should be available to the kubelet prior to applications running for a number of features to work
 - Downwards API (both volume and environment variables) rely on this
 - [INLINE_CODE] file, created by kubelet, relies on this (alternately, rkt should create this correctly)
- The network plugin configuration used by the docker container runtime should work, in general, for rkt with no changes (including filepath) (https://github.com/coreos/rkt/issues/2249)
- The solution should work with any rkt stage1 (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/26081)
## Solutions
1. Rkt manages the network
2. Kubelet manages the network
3. Hybrid of 1 & 2
### Rkt manages networking

This option has a few problems:
1. The PodIP is not available to the kubelet until after the application is finalized (including mounts and environment variables) (https://github.com/coreos/rkt/issues/2223 and https://github.com/coreos/rkt/issues/2375)
2. The network plugin configuration path is not configurable (https://github.com/coreos/rkt/pull/2312)
3. Duplication of logic/code between kubelet and rkt (more or less depending on who creates [INLINE_CODE] and so on).

The first issue there is a difficult one to solve and is the main reason that this approach was discarded, whether temporarily or not.

This is probably the only robust long-term solution when considering the large variety of stage1's (and thus network configurations) that are available and, once rkt provides a container-level interface (see https://github.com/coreos/rkt/issues/2375), there should be a natural way to solve problem number one via the separation of sandbox creation and container creation.
### Kubelet manages networking

This option has its own problems:
1. Does not work with kvm flavor stage1 (or any stage1 that does not use Linux network namespaces or does not support [INLINE_CODE]).
2. Depends on availability of nsenter / ip tools (already depended on elsewhere I believe, mostly a nonissue)
3. Results in the [INLINE_CODE] cli reporting incorrect network information

This allows fulfilling more of kubelet's assumptions about networking, but does not play nicely with rkt's existing abstractions. It does solve the most problems for the case of the default stage1 and existing rkt featureset while also not being a large amount of code. It also shares significant logic with the docker network setup, with the benefits that entails.
### Hybrid

The kubelet could decide whether it or rkt should manage the networking based on whether the stage1 suports it. When rkt manages networking, the features dependent on PodIP being available early on will not work.
1. More code in kubelet to support both methods
2. rkt does not provide an easy means to determine whether one or the other is appropriate currently
3. Inconsistent featureset depending on stage1 (:frowning:)
## Conclusion

My current preference is to continue with the kubelet-managed network for 1.0 (though given the timeline, I'm not sure there's another choice), and rethink this afterwards. If it's possible to support a hybrid approach by 1.0 with the understanding that it's a temporary solution, that also seems reasonable.

Ideally, the kubelet's abstractions would not interfere with rkt's ability to manage networking itself since, I admit, the above solution is a bit of a hacky one.

It's also possible that the upcoming Container Runtime Interface changes, with a focus on sandboxes, will require further changes in both the kubelet and rkt that changes what issues are present.

I'd like to gather other's thoughts and make sure we're all on the same page and figure out if there are other options or issues I'm not thinking of.

/cc @yifan-gu @jellonek @pskrzyns @jonboulle @dcbw @iaguis @philips @thockin @freehan

Volumes remain attached to a node when kubelet on the node is unexpectedly terminated (because, for example, the node was restarted). When a node becomes inaccessible, the scheduler, schedules the pods from the downed node to another node. However, certain volumes can only be attached to one node at a time (for example GCE PDs may only be attached to one instance in RW mode). Pods that require a volume that can only be attached to a single node will be unable to start once rescheduled to a new node, because their volume can not be attached to the new node since it was never detached from the old node.

See issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/14642
# Potential Solutions
1. Node detaches from other node
 - If a node detects that it is unable to attach a device because it is attached to another node, the node should detach it from the other node, and retry attaching it.
 - Cons: Could lead to two nodes fighting each other for a volume.
2. Garbage collection on node
 - Cons: Can’t rely on the node to to do cleanup: for example garbage collection can’t happen if the plug is pulled on a node.
3. Node Fencing
 - The logic on the scheduler that currently determines if a node is up or down and reschedules pods, should also trigger resource reclamation from downed nodes (detaching disks as well as potentially other clean up).
 - Cons: Decoupling attachment and detachment leads to inherent race conditions, as long as the node itself can decide to attach a volume to itself.
4. Volume Attachment/Detachment Controller
 - Move the volume attachment/detachment logic from kubelet to a separate off-node controller (maybe running on master or as a pod).
# Proposal

I think the “Volume Attachment/Detachment Controller” would be the most robust design.

A node should not be responsible for determining whether to attach or detach a volume to itself. Instead the responsibility should be moved (out of kubelet) to a separate off-node “Volume Attachment/Detachment Controller”.

This controller would keep track of:
- Which pods require which volumes.
- Which nodes these pods have been scheduled to.
- Which volumes have been successfully attached to which nodes.

The controller would be responsible for attaching a volume to a node if:
- A pod with a volume is scheduled to a node and the volume is not already attached to the node (no existing pod on the node requires the volume).
- The volumes policy permits attachment to multiple nodes, or the volumes policy permits attachment only to a single node and there are no other nodes that the volume is already attached to.

The controller would be responsible for detaching a volume from a node if:
- There are no pods running on the node using that volume.

Some volume types may not have a concept of attaching to a node (e.g. NFS volume), and for these volume types the attach and detach methods should be no-ops.

Another benefit of this approach is that it allows the controller to ensure that attach and detach do not occur simultaneously for a particular volume (avoiding lots of horrible race conditions).
## Open questions:
- Mount/unmount code must still exist on the node. How does the controller signal to the node that a volume is attached along with sufficient information (mount dir, etc.) for the node to mount it?
 - Could the mounting logic be dumb and just constantly poll a location on a disk? Would it work for all existing and future volumes?
 - Could the attach/detach logic update the PVC/PV object with some state indicating the nodes it is attached to?
- How do you make this controller plugable?
 - As we proposed for the dynamic volume provisioning controller.
 - For v1 all plugins are compiled in (as is the case for existing volume “plugins”).
 - For v2 anyone can implement their own attachment/detachment controller by creating a binary/pod/script/etc. that:
 - Monitoring API server for pod, node, and PVC/PV objects.
 - Writing updates to these objects

results.query_title: Add priority function for NodeNotReady count to probabalistically quarantine flapping nodes safely
results.query_body:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/19118#issuecomment-172102534 refers.

I think that we should potentially have a mechanism in place for quarantining nodes that fail often/repeatedly. We will of course need to be careful of "poisoned pods" which, when launched on a node, cause it to fail often and get quarantined. If the poison pod then gets rescheduled to another node in the cluster, eventually all nodes could become quarantined. That would be very bad. But repeated hardware or system problems on a node should ultimately cause pods not to scheduled there, somehow, safely.

A good approach might be to use a basic [priority function](kubernetes/docs/devel/scheduler.md). For example, keep a sliding window not ready count per node (how many times a node has gone not ready in a given time window), and add a priority function to put nodes with high not ready counts at the bottom of the list when selecting nodes. That works around the poisoned pod problem outlined above, as we wouldn't actually lose real capacity by hard quarantining nodes. Only probabalistically avoid scheduling onto more flaky nodes. I think that's both simple and effective. Unless @mml or @davidopp have better ideas, I think that we should add this feature to the backlog.

results.query_body:
# Objective
- Rapid pod creation, deletion, and recreation for pods that require volume attaching/detaching/mounting/unmounting should never fail because of attach/detach/mount/unmount issues.
- Volumes that are attached/mounted should be gracefully handled on kubelet restart.
 - Issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/19953
- Two or more pods scheduled to the same node with the same volume should never fail (as long as it is allowed by the volume plugin’s AccessModes policy).
 - Issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/19953
- When a volume is attached to the node in read-only mode, and the pod referencing it is deleted and another pod referencing the volume is quickly created in read-write mode, then the volume should detached and reattached in the correct (read-write) mode.
 - Issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/11879
- One or more pods referencing different partitions of the same volume should not fail (as long as it doesn’t violate volume plugin’s AccessModes policy).
 - Issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/20835
# Background

In the existing Kubernetes design the kubelet is responsible for determining what volumes to attach/mount and detach/unmount from the node it is running on.

The loop in Kubelet that is responsible for attaching and mounting volumes (the pod creation loop) is separate from and completely independent (on a separate thread) of the loop that is responsible for unmounting and detaching volumes (orphaned volumes loop). This leads to race conditions between the asynchronous pod creation and orphaned volumes loops.

Although there is some logic in the GCE PD, AWS, and Cinder plugins to make sure that the actual attach/detach operations don’t interrupt each other, there is no guarantee as to the order of the operations themselves. So, for example, when a pod is created and then rapidly deleted and recreated, kubelet attaches and mounts the pod, then (if the second attach operation is triggered before the detach operation, which often happens) kubelet will execute the second attach operation successfully (since the disk is already attached), and the pending detach operation will then result in a disk-in-use being unmounted (which appears like data loss to user).

To mask this behavior, kubelet currently fails attach operations if the disk is already attached. This allows the second attach operation to fail, and the subsequent detach operation to succeed; further retries of the attach operation then succeed.

Although this workaround masks a nasty bug (apparent data loss to the end user), it results in other unwanted behavior (bugs):
1. When a kubelet is restarted, pods with volumes that are already attached will fail to start, because attempts by kubelet to attach a volume that is already attached continuously fail (since the volume is already attached).
2. When two or more pods specify the same volume (allowed for some plugins in certain cases), the second pod will fail to start because because the volume attach call for the 2nd pod will continuously fail since the volume is already attached (by the first pod).

The Volume/Attach Detach Controller design (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/20262) plans to move the attach/detach logic from kubelet to master, however the kubelet will still be responsible for mounting/unmounting (and, for backwards compatibility reasons, attach/detach in some cases), therefore these issues must be addressed.
# Solution Overview

Introduce a new asynchronous loop, called the volume manager loop, in kubelet that handles attach/detach and mount/unmount in a serialized manner. The existing orphaned volumes loop will be removed, and the logic for unmounting/detaching volumes will be moved to the volume manager loop. Similarly, the logic for determining which volumes to mount/attach will be moved from the pod creation loop to the volume manager loop. The pod creation loop will simply poll the new volume manager until its volumes are ready for use (attached and mounted).
# Detailed Design

The volume manager will maintain an in-memory cache containing a list of volumes that are required by the node (i.e. volumes that are referenced by pods scheduled to the node that the kubelet is running on). Each of these volumes will, in addition to the volume name, specify if the volume is mounted in read-only mode, and list the pods referencing the volume. This cache defines the state of the world according to the volume manager. This cache must be thread-safe.

On initial startup, the volume manager will read the [INLINE_CODE] and [INLINE_CODE] directories to figure out which volumes were attached and mounted to the node before it went down and pre-populate the in-memory cache.
### Primary Control Loop

The volume manager will have a loop that does the following:
- Fetch a copy of all pod and mirror pod objects from kubelet via pod manager.
- Acquire a lock on the in-memory cache.
- Search for new pods by iterating through the fetched pods, and for each pod with a [INLINE_CODE] [INLINE_CODE] check the volumes it defines or references (dereferencing any [INLINE_CODE] to fetch associated [INLINE_CODE] objects). For each of these volume:
 - If the volume _is not_ already in-memory cache (indicating a new volume has been discovered), then:
 - **Trigger “attach volume and mount device” logic** (detailed in section below) to attach the volume to the node and mount it to the main mount location.
 - A matching volume must also match access mode. For example, if a volume was attached in read-only mode, a new pod referencing the same volume in read-write mode, will be treated as a separate volume (this enables the scenario mentioned in objectives above).
 - If the volume is _already tracked_ in memory cache (indicating it is already attached and mounted to main location), then:

- Search for terminated/deleted pods by looping through all cached pods (i.e. volume->pods) and **trigger “unmount bind mount” logic** for the volume(s) defined for that pod, if:

- Loop through all cached volumes and **trigger “unmount device and detach volume” logic** (detailed below) for any volumes that are no longer needed (exist in-memory cache but have no pods listed under them, indicating no running pods using the volume).

Instead the primary loop should spawn new threads for these operations. The number of threads that can be spawned will be capped (possibly using a thread pool) and once the cap is hit, subsequent requests will have to wait for a thread to become available.

To prevent multiple attach/detach or mount/unmount operations on the same volume, the main thread will maintain a table mapping volumes to currently active operations.

results.query_title: rkt networking discussion
results.query_body:
There are a number of small pieces of discussion scattered across this and the rkt repository related to how to handle networking setup; I'd like to consolidate this discussion here, talk about all the issues and options I know about, and hopefully figure out what the best option is.

Discussion refs:
https://github.com/coreos/rkt/issues/2249
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/26081
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/25404#issuecomment-218402169
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/24688
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/21923
And quite possibly several more I missed
## Introduction

Kubernetes and rkt both make use of CNI to configure container network namespaces. Each has independent means of configuring and executing plugins. Kubernetes also has a number of features that relate somewhat to the network namespace, such as availability of the pod's IP in a number of locations (status, downwards API, etc).

Until recently, rkt's handled network configuration on its own with no regard for Kubernetes' network logic. As of #25062, it was changed such that kubelet handles network setup and configuration for rkt. Unfortunately, both of these solutions have problems.

Below, the problems with each approach are listed. Finally, some paths forwards are suggested.
## Issues
- The PodIP should be available to the kubelet prior to applications running for a number of features to work
 - Downwards API (both volume and environment variables) rely on this
 - [INLINE_CODE] file, created by kubelet, relies on this (alternately, rkt should create this correctly)
- The network plugin configuration used by the docker container runtime should work, in general, for rkt with no changes (including filepath) (https://github.com/coreos/rkt/issues/2249)
- The solution should work with any rkt stage1 (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/26081)
## Solutions
1. Rkt manages the network
2. Kubelet manages the network
3. Hybrid of 1 & 2
### Rkt manages networking

This option has a few problems:
1. The PodIP is not available to the kubelet until after the application is finalized (including mounts and environment variables) (https://github.com/coreos/rkt/issues/2223 and https://github.com/coreos/rkt/issues/2375)
2. The network plugin configuration path is not configurable (https://github.com/coreos/rkt/pull/2312)
3. Duplication of logic/code between kubelet and rkt (more or less depending on who creates [INLINE_CODE] and so on).

The first issue there is a difficult one to solve and is the main reason that this approach was discarded, whether temporarily or not.

This is probably the only robust long-term solution when considering the large variety of stage1's (and thus network configurations) that are available and, once rkt provides a container-level interface (see https://github.com/coreos/rkt/issues/2375), there should be a natural way to solve problem number one via the separation of sandbox creation and container creation.
### Kubelet manages networking

This option has its own problems:
1. Does not work with kvm flavor stage1 (or any stage1 that does not use Linux network namespaces or does not support [INLINE_CODE]).
2. Depends on availability of nsenter / ip tools (already depended on elsewhere I believe, mostly a nonissue)
3. Results in the [INLINE_CODE] cli reporting incorrect network information

This allows fulfilling more of kubelet's assumptions about networking, but does not play nicely with rkt's existing abstractions. It does solve the most problems for the case of the default stage1 and existing rkt featureset while also not being a large amount of code. It also shares significant logic with the docker network setup, with the benefits that entails.
### Hybrid

The kubelet could decide whether it or rkt should manage the networking based on whether the stage1 suports it. When rkt manages networking, the features dependent on PodIP being available early on will not work.
1. More code in kubelet to support both methods
2. rkt does not provide an easy means to determine whether one or the other is appropriate currently
3. Inconsistent featureset depending on stage1 (:frowning:)
## Conclusion

My current preference is to continue with the kubelet-managed network for 1.0 (though given the timeline, I'm not sure there's another choice), and rethink this afterwards. If it's possible to support a hybrid approach by 1.0 with the understanding that it's a temporary solution, that also seems reasonable.

Ideally, the kubelet's abstractions would not interfere with rkt's ability to manage networking itself since, I admit, the above solution is a bit of a hacky one.

It's also possible that the upcoming Container Runtime Interface changes, with a focus on sandboxes, will require further changes in both the kubelet and rkt that changes what issues are present.

I'd like to gather other's thoughts and make sure we're all on the same page and figure out if there are other options or issues I'm not thinking of.

/cc @yifan-gu @jellonek @pskrzyns @jonboulle @dcbw @iaguis @philips @thockin @freehan

results.query_body:
_Note: Relates to issue [#28310: Discovering, bookkeeping and isolating platform resources other than CPU time and main memory.](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/28310)_

_See also: [#28311: Hardware feature discovery to add node labels with a unique prefix (e.g. [INLINE_CODE]).](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/28311)_

This issue tracks work related to opaque counted (integer) resources.

Many opaque resources have a shareable capacity and can’t be represented well as a label. An “opaque integer resource” mechanism could work for these resources.

**What are some example use cases for opaque integer resources?**
- LLC (last-level cache) allocation.
- GPU devices
- FPGA devices
- MICs (Many-Integrated Core, such as Xeon Phi)
- “Slots” for sharing bandwidth to a parallel file system.

**Who discovers and publishes these opaque node resources?**
- Option 1: A sidecar pod running on every node publishes capacity in [INLINE_CODE]
- Option 2: Kubelet discovers and publishes capacity in [INLINE_CODE]

**How would opaque integer resources be accounted?**

The scheduler could compute the free resource amount by deducting the sum of requests from capacity, for use in pod feasibility checks. This is similar to the existing code paths for cpu time and memory resources.

For user experience and possibly scheduling we may want to report usage in addition to capacity (for resources where usage can be <= the allocated amount). This could be handled via the Heapster/metrics API.

results.query_title: DESIGN: External IPs
results.query_body:
## Goal

To evaluate options for connecting “external” IP addresses to kubernetes-hosted applications.
## Non-Goals

To discuss the kubernetes Service abstraction (mostly, see #1107).
## Background

Running Pods and Services within a kubernetes cluster is fairly well defined (or becoming so).  A frequent question, though, is how to publish something to the “outside world” (for which the definition varies depending on the hosting situation).  Today we have a Service.CreateExternalLoadBalancer flag, which tells kubernetes to invoke cloud-provider logic to establish a load balancer across all minions on the service port on the minion’s interface.  This port is answered by the kube-proxy, which does it’s own round-robin “balancing”.

This design was easy to establish as a prototype, but is problematic for the long term because it depends on a flat service-port namespace, which we want to make go away (see #1107), and because it uses two levels of balancing, which is not good for performance or predictability.

We should be able to establish a more performant and direct pattern for externalizing kubernetes-hosted applications.
## Design

There are a few ways this could be done.  The remainder of this doc will explore the trade-offs.  I will describe the need for external access as an external port, rather than an external IP.  This leaves the implementations free to optimize IP usage, if needed.
### Option 1) Flag some services as “external”, run load balancers inside k8s

Services carry a flag indicating the need for an external port.  When a Service is created with this flag set, the kubernetes master will spin up a new pod (call it a “service pod”) which runs a kubernetes-aware balancer (this might just be kube-proxy or an enlightened HAProxy or ...).  Like all pods, this pod must be managed by a controller (call it a “service controller”) and is given a pod IP address.  The controller for this pod has the responsibility to reach out to the cloud provider and provision an external port which forwards to the service pod’s IP.  Whatever portal solution we decide to use (see #1107) would forward to this service pod.  If the service pod is relocated, the service controller may need to update the cloud provider.

Pros:
- Fairly consistent experience across cloud providers
- Same implementation, minus external, can be used for “real” internal load balancing

Cons:
- Less obvious how to integrate real cloud-provider load-balancing
- Users don’t get to choose their balancing solution
 - could be mitigated by extra fields in Service
- Expensive for singleton pods that want an external port
 - could be mitigated by changing the external flag to indicate N=1 vs N>1
### Option 2) Flag some services as “external”, let cloudprovider define the meaning

Similar to option 1, but more abstract.  Services carry a flag indicating the need for an external port.  When a Service is created with this flag set, the kubernetes master will reach out to the cloud provider and provision an external service.  The cloud provider modules would determine what this means.  For the simplest cases, this could be implemented the same as option 1.  For cloud providers that can use native load balancers, this could be implemented in terms of them.

Pros:
- As an abstraction, provides freedom to evolve the implementation
- Sets a pattern for internal load balancing as a function of cloud provider

Cons:
- Less consistent across cloud providers
- Users don’t get to choose their balancing solution
 - could be mitigated by extra fields in Service
- Expensive for singleton pods that want an external port
 - could be mitigated by changing the external flag to indicate N=1 vs N>1
### Option 3) Any pod can be flagged as “external”, users set up their own balancing

Similar to option 2, but not tied to Services.  Pods carry a flag indicating the need for an external port.  When a Pod is created with this flag set, the kubernetes master will reach out to the cloud provider and provision an external port.  The cloud provider modules would determine what this means.  The end user is responsible for setting up the pod to be a load balancer, though we can make kube-proxy be suitable for this purpose.  Because this is a plain pod, it needs to be run under a controller, itself - probably a replication controller of N=1.  In order for this pattern to hold for internal load balancing, the user would need another Service with a Portal (see #1107) that forwards to it.

Pros:
- Users can configure anything they want as their balancer
- This is the underlying form of options 1 and 2 anyway
- Conceptually simple
- Very composable
- Works well for singleton pods that want an external IP but don’t need balancing

Cons:
- Forces users to set up balancing themselves
- Less obvious how to integrate real cloud-provider load-balancing
- Not obvious which master module is responsible for syncing external IP to internal IP when the pod is relocated
- Internal use through Portals (See #1107) would be an extra hop (kube-proxy + load balancer) since it is not part of the Service abstraction
 - could be mitigated with a new kind of Service, “singleton” or something to make a direct portal

Right now JSONBase, which includes Kind, ID, CreationTimestamp, SelfLink, ResourceVersion, and APIVersion, is returned in most API responses, including lists (GET of collection URLs), in particular. Client-initiated terminations are triggered by DELETE via the API. As discussed in #137, I'd like clients to be able to pass in arbitrary termination reasons, to facilitate ecosystem management extensions, as well as user-provided reasons.

results.query_title: Configuration reconciliation (aka kubectl apply)
results.query_body:
Forked from #1007 and #1325 .

We want to support management of services via declarative configuration. 

The configuration files written by the user may need to undergo multiple transformations before submitting them to the API, as discussed in #1694, but the result of these steps should be concrete objects. These objects may need to be created, updated, and/or deleted.

On an object-by-object basis, it should be possible via kubectl (via a client library) to do the following:
1. Determine whether or not the specified object already exists
2. Get the specified object
3. Create the specified object
4. Diff the specified object with an existing object in apiserver
5. Update an existing object in apiserver with the data from the specified object
6. Delete the specified object
7. Delete all objects with deployment-specific labels (see #1698)

The configured fields should be recorded in the object via annotations, as discussed in #1178 and #1201. Only the previously and newly configured fields, labels, and annotations should be diff'ed and/or updated. Other fields from the existing object should be ignored/merged, and the set of configured fields should be updated with each update.

We ultimately do want to automate most of the orchestration/workflow involved in deployment. However, this is fairly complex, and we can't necessarily automate all of it in a domain-independent, use-case-independent manner. In general, a full deployment would likely be comprised of multiple files, each containing multiple objects. These objects may have inter-dependencies (e.g., right now services must be created before their clients are created), rolling updates require special treatment (#1353), and application-specific rollout logic may be required. Therefore, I recommend we keep the more general deployment workflow separate from the basic primitive mechanism that reconciles a single object, and ensure that the two are composable. I'll file another issue for the workflow part.

Among other things, composition means that the invoker of the tool and/or library needs to be able to distinguish noop (e.g., object already exists and matches config), success, retryable failure, and permanent failure, so the overall workflow can decide what to do after each step.

We ultimately want to automate most of the orchestration/workflow involved in deployment, so that most users don't need to write custom workflows or scripts. However, it's fairly complex, and we can't necessarily automate all of it in a domain-independent, use-case-independent manner.

results.query_title: Securing kubernetes-ro use cases
results.query_body:
We'd like all communications to the apiserver to be over https and with authorization.
Kubernetes-ro does not meet these standards.

This bug is about things that use the kubernetes-ro service or the KUBERNETES_RO_\* env vars.
kube-proxy is discussed separately in #5917 since it explicitly uses port explicitly 7080 and has a straightforward fix.
## Existing Uses

Use cases for kubernetes-ro
1. cluster/addons/dns/kube2sky/kube2sky.go
2. cluster/addons/fluentd-elasticsearch/logging-demo/README.md
3. examples/cassandra/java/io/k8s/cassandra/KubernetesSeedProvider.java
4. examples/phabricator/cloudsql-authenticator/run.sh
5. examples/rethinkdb/image/run.sh
6. examples/rethinkdb/image/run.sh 
7. contrib/for-tests/network-tester/webserver.go
8. users have said they use kubernetes-ro.
## Backwards Compatibile or Breakage?

In order to make this be https, we have to break some uses cases, because some existing use cases assume it is http. So, we could either have a breakage day, or have it be configurable at cluster setup time, and just move GCE/GKE to the https option. The latter seems expedient but it would force some code like kube2sky and elasticsearch to handle both options. Better to just break it.

Decision: breakage.
## Credential distribution

We need to distribute credentials to clients. The use cases are in pods, so we need a way to distribute credentials to all pods that need them. Credentials would probably be in the form of a kubernetes_auth file. 

We could use [INLINE_CODE] to distribute the kubernetes_auth files. This does make some of the pod descriptions quite a bit mode verbose. But we can address that later using service accounts or config templates/expansions.
### credential creation
1. In the place where we create a "kubelet" token, also create a token for user "readonlyuser". 
2. Put this token into a kubernetes_auth file.
3. Put the kubernetes_auth file along with the master's certificates into a [INLINE_CODE] object.
4. Post this secret to the master in [INLINE_CODE]. 
### credential use
1. Change all pods that currently reference kubernetes-ro/KUBERNETES_RO to have a secret volume source. 
2. Change all the go code that references KUBERNETES_RO to instead take a [INLINE_CODE] flag.
3. change the java code and shell code to extract master address and the auth token and the certs from the kubernetes_auth file and use https.
4. change all the shell code that uses KUBERNETES_RO and [INLINE_CODE] to extract the auth token from the kubernetes_auth 
### Cleanup
1. Stop advertising kubernetes-ro service (remove from pkg/master/publish.go)
2. fix docs to never speak of it again.

As an initial step, every cluster should be built with a secret with user [INLINE_CODE] 
### Alternative

Run a proxy on each node which listens on each netns's localhost address, or one some other address visible to all netnses. Listen for http. Proxy via HTTPS to the master. See #2209

Advantages:
- no credentials to distribute to pods, and to perhaps be compromised
- no verbosity in pods for the secret volume source
- no breakage for users
 Disadvantages:
 - fixing urls in proxies
 - unforseen complexity with proxying.
 - uses a special mechanism for kubernetes auth, instead of the the more general option we expect users to use (Secrets).
 - more moving parts. more magic, instead of well-understood, composable mechanisms.
